title: Pairing metrics with multiples
objectives: Answer out loud: Why can't you use EV/Net income?
Answer out loud: What are EBITDA's weaknesses?
Answer out loud: When use EV/revenue?

steps.body: The **consistency rule:** the numerator and denominator must refer to the same group of investors.
EV (all investors) pairs with metrics *before* interest: revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, unlevered FCF.
Equity value (shareholders only) pairs with metrics *after* interest: net income (P/E), EPS, levered FCF.

blocks.template: EV / {{1}} is valid; EV / {{2}} is not
For an unprofitable company, use EV / {{1}}

blocks.title: Why can't you use EV / Net income?
blocks.teaser: EV covers all investors, but net income is what's left after debt holders get paid interest.
blocks.body:
EV covers all investors, but net income is what's left *after* debt holders get paid interest. The numerator includes debt holders; the denominator excludes them.

**Interview answer:** "EV belongs to all investors, but net income only belongs to shareholders, since interest is already paid. The two don't match."

blocks.explanation: EV belongs to all investors; net income is after interest, so it belongs only to shareholders. The numerator and denominator don't match.

blocks.title: Why is EV/EBITDA so popular?
blocks.teaser: It's capital-structure neutral (comparable across companies with different debt), unaffected by tax differences, and EBITDA roughly proxies operating…
blocks.body: It's capital-structure neutral (comparable across companies with different debt), unaffected by tax differences, and EBITDA roughly proxies operating cash flow. It's the default for most industries.

blocks.title: What are EBITDA's weaknesses?
blocks.teaser: It ignores CapEx (a company with huge capital needs looks better than it is), working capital, taxes, and SBC if added back.
blocks.body:
It ignores CapEx (a company with huge capital needs looks better than it is), working capital, taxes, and SBC if added back. For capital-intensive businesses, EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA − CapEx) is more honest.

**Interview answer:** "It ignores CapEx and working capital, so it flatters capital-intensive businesses. For them I'd look at EV/EBIT or EBITDA minus CapEx."

blocks.title: Why is P/E distorted by capital structure?
blocks.teaser: Two identical businesses with different debt levels have different interest costs, so different net income, so different P/E.
blocks.body: Two identical businesses with different debt levels have different interest costs, so different net income, so different P/E. EV/EBITDA strips that out.

blocks.title: Why might two companies with similar growth trade at different EV/EBITDA multiples?
blocks.teaser: Differences in margins, return on capital (how much reinvestment growth requires), risk/cyclicality, capital intensity, quality of management, or bus…
blocks.body: Differences in margins, return on capital (how much reinvestment growth requires), risk/cyclicality, capital intensity, quality of management, or business model durability. Growth alone doesn't determine the multiple.

blocks.title: What's the PEG ratio?
blocks.body: P/E ÷ expected EPS growth rate. It adjusts P/E for growth so fast- and slow-growing companies can be compared. A PEG around 1.0 is often read as "fair."
